title: the dice game
hook: the brothers staked one by one, Yudhishthira himself, and then Draupadi
carry: name it plainly, the way he did

segments.voice: Yesterday in the dice game, the drumbeat of I have won, and Vidura's man reaching for honey. Did you look for the edge of a streak? Day seven hundred sixty-nine.

Every treasure is gone. In the telling, Yudhishthira stakes his herds, his lands, his city, even the ornaments the princes wear. Lost, every one. And then the game changes from a matter of things to a matter of people. Shakuni asks, is there anything left? There is. Sitting near Yudhishthira, listening to all of it, are his four brothers. Today, the last stakes of the dice game, and the moment the hall is shaken.
screen: `EVERY TREASURE IS GONE.` → `IS THERE ANYTHING LEFT?` → `HIS FOUR BROTHERS.`

segments.voice: Yudhishthira stakes Nakula, one of the twins. Shakuni throws, and wins. He stakes the other twin, Sahadeva. Lost. Then Shakuni tries something sly. The twins, he says, are Madri's sons. Surely Bhima and Arjuna, Kunti's sons, your own mother's sons, are dearer to you. You won't stake them. It's an attempt to split the brothers along their mothers' line. And Yudhishthira, losing everything, still catches it. He says, in effect: you're trying to divide us, and that's wrong. Then, as if to show they can't be divided, he stakes Arjuna. Lost. He stakes Bhima. Lost. He stakes himself. Lost. Shakuni says there's still one stake left: Draupadi. And Yudhishthira stakes her, describing her goodness as he does. Now the poem turns to the room. The elders, Bhishma, Drona and Kripa, are shaken; the telling says they break into a sweat. Vidura holds his head in his hands. The blind king, who can't see the board, keeps asking whether the throw has been won. Shakuni throws. And he wins. Look at the strange shape of that last streak. Yudhishthira's loyalty to his brothers is real. He refuses to let Shakuni set them against each other. And that same loyalty is what he puts on the board, one brother after another. A virtue and a disaster in the same breath. The stakes run out here, with a woman lost in a game she never sat down to play. What she does next turns the hall upside down.
screen: `THE TWINS, ONE AFTER THE OTHER.` · `SHAKUNI TRIES TO DIVIDE THE BROTHERS.` · `ARJUNA, BHIMA, HIMSELF.` · `DRAUPADI IS STAKED.` · then, large: `THE HALL IS SHAKEN.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let the shoulders soften. Bring to mind the people you'd stand up for without thinking: a sibling, a friend, a partner, a child. Let their faces come one at a time. Notice how it feels simply to hold them in mind, none of them on any table, none of them part of any bet. Breathe in with one face, and out with the next. If you pray, you can hold each of them in your prayer. If not, simply wish each of them well. The bell holds the time.
Pana, a wager. Brothers are staked one by one, a king loses himself, and Draupadi is lost in a game she never played.
Your line: name it plainly, the way he did. Today, if someone tries to set you against a person you love, name it plainly, the way Yudhishthira did. Day seven hundred sixty-nine.

howItsDone: The last stakes of the dice game are read aloud and staged as a turning point of the epic.

fork.setup: you're Yudhishthira. Shakuni says you'll never stake Kunti's sons, since they must be dearer to you than the twins. what do you do?
options: call it an attempt to divide you, and stake Arjuna.
fork.reveal: he calls Shakuni's words wrong for trying to split the brothers, then stakes Arjuna, then Bhima, then himself, and loses every throw.

original.note: Sanskrit paṇa: a wager, the stake put down in a game.

trapdoor: what you thought: a gambler who didn't care about his family.
what it means: a brother loyal enough to refuse Shakuni's divide, who still puts each brother on the board.
what a scholar hears: Yudhishthira stakes himself before Draupadi, and that order is the seed of the question she will ask.
